title: Kid Rene's trumpet and the Brown Derby; battle of the bands on trucks
summary: Kid Rene played high above the staff and later worked with Bigard at the Brown Derby; bands used to buck against each other on the streets.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Buddy Bolden and Buddy Petit: the trumpet legends

blocks.x: But not loud, they say. No, he wasn't quite loud, but he was pretty good. He was pretty good. Now what about other trumpet players there around the time you were playing with Buddy? Would they play a whole mamba or would they take it down? Oh yeah, you'd take like this little fella there, Kid René, when I was telling you about it. He was about one of the best trumpet players around there to my estimation. He would only take one course, he'd take two chords. He'd take it above the staff. And stay above the staff. You ain't never heard nobody play high society above the staff. He'd take two steps to stay there. He's one of your little greatest there around here. He'd play with me until he died. We worked at the Brown Derby on Canal Street.
Well I was there, I heard you. You heard me? Yeah, I think I was in the Navy then, or maybe I was on vacation.
Yeah, and Morgan was there. Morgan was there. And Black Benny Turner. That's right, that's right. And I went down to see Big Eye at Lutchen's, I remember that. Yeah, that's right.

And you played Royal Garden Blues and Sister Kate. That's right. I can remember that. But then he was a sick man during the time you'd say anything, he was a sick man. But he made it on those last courses.
Oh yeah. He could give out. Much better than his records. Oh yeah. You ever heard his records? No. He was playing in the middle right just to play straight lead practically, huh Bill?

Doesn't really get cut loose, you know. He was tough. He was tough. When he was in his prime, and these bands would be out here on these advertising, and they'd tell you a little turk, we used to call them little turk, you see a little turk at the next corner, they'd support the passing block, they'd make a round of blood. Because the bands used to stay there and buck for another hour. An hour and a half. Just like you're playing for a dance. Yeah. So one would make up their mind and go.
